entries.tech_name: Genomic Selection for Low Methane Traits

second_rater.rationale: Genomic selection for low methane traits has transitioned from research to commercial deployment, highlighted by Canada's Lactanet launching the first national genetic evaluation for methane efficiency in April 2023, which is currently used across 6,000 farms representing 60% of Canadian dairy operations (t007-selecting-methane-traits_e060, t007-selecting-methane-traits_e181, t007-selecting-methane-traits_e219). Similar genetic selection programs and tools are also active in New Zealand and the Nordic region (t007-selecting-methane-traits_e282, t007-selecting-methane-traits_e372).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Canada's Lactanet officially launched the world's first national single-step genomic evaluation for methane efficiency (MEF) in the Holstein breed in April 2023, yielding Relative Breeding Values at >70% reliability and covering over 6,000 farms representing ~60% of Canadian dairy operations (e054, e060, e181, e219). In New Zealand, selection lines for low-methane sheep are maintained commercially and at least one breeder reports a 3.2% herd methane reduction over four years of active selection (e167, e372, e371). These deployments confirm the technology is operating at scale in real-world production environments. Remaining constraints—limited reference populations for beef and non-dairy sectors, reliance on MIR proxies rather than direct measurement, and acknowledged need for further farmer education (e012, e041, e092, e330)—indicate the system is not yet fully proven across all species and geographies, placing it at TRL 7–8 rather than 9.

second_rater.rationale: Bio-preservation via phages and metabolites is fully commercialized and deployed in the real world, with multiple FDA-cleared and USDA-approved products such as ListShield™ and PhageGuard-E targeting Listeria and E. coli in food processing environments (t070-phage-biopreservation_e171, t070-phage-biopreservation_e246, t070-phage-biopreservation_e248, t070-phage-biopreservation_e356). Additionally, metabolite-based biopreservatives like nisin have been FDA-approved and used extensively in industrial settings since 1988 (t070-phage-biopreservation_e121, t070-phage-biopreservation_e552, t070-phage-biopreservation_e563).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Multiple commercial phage-based food safety products have received full regulatory approval and are actively deployed in real food processing environments. ListShield™ received FDA GRAS clearance in 2006 (e246); PhageGuard Listex was approved by FSANZ in 2011 and evaluated by EFSA (e247); PhageGuard-E was certified GRAS by FDA/USDA in 2018 for beef carcass decontamination (e248); and SalmoFresh™/EcoShield™ are commercially applied via industrial sprayers achieving 99–99.9% pathogen reductions in actual processing facilities (e171, e172, e356). Bacteriocin-based biopreservation (nisin) is even more mature, having been FDA-approved since 1988 and commercially used since the 1950s across dairy, meat, and vegetable applications at global industrial scale (e121, e552, e553, e563). Real-world poultry processor deployments, fresh-cut produce rinse programs, and smoked-fish facility interventions are documented (e250, e252, e253, e254), confirming the full system operates routinely in operational environments. Some ongoing challenges—phage resistance emergence, formulation stability in high-temperature settings, gaps in coverage for certain pathogens—prevent a uniform TRL 9 designation for all sub-applications (e225, e226, e441), but the technology as a whole is proven functional in use.

second_rater.rationale: While conventional probiotics have established pathways, engineered microbes must navigate complex and fragmented regulatory frameworks. The US USDA has pioneered a licensing plan for BE-101 (a genetically engineered input) and approved master seeds, though it still requires risk analysis and field safety studies. Other major jurisdictions like the EU, China, and Australia maintain rigid, multi-layered GMO or novel feed regulations that create significant delays.

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The conventional probiotic sub-component (Bacillus spp., yeast-based DFMs) enjoys well-established regulatory pathways in the US (AAFCO ingredient definitions and FDA GRAS framework, e536/e537/e248) and the EU (Regulation 1831/2003, 220+ EFSA-validated products, e116/e148/e337), which alone would support a High bin. However, the defining and novel aspect of this technology—native rumen microbes engineered for permanent/semi-permanent microbiome reprogramming—remains squarely in the navigation phase: in the US, BE-101 is explicitly described as 'the first product of its kind' regulated by USDA, with the Federal Register process (risk analysis, public comment, field safety studies) still underway rather than completed (e059, e065). The EU imposes protracted, process-based GMO authorization with only one GM crop approved for cultivation since 2000 (e514), and multi-agency overlap under Regulation 1829/2003 (e505/e507); China requires dual-track review under both novel feed and GM safety legislation (e511); and Australia's system is described as fragmented and onerous (e515). CRISPR-based rumen engineering faces explicitly noted 'regulatory and ethical considerations' as a remaining substantial challenge (e051), and no specific frameworks exist for multi-strain engineered consortia (e073). The most favorable jurisdiction (US) for the engineered component supports Mid-level navigation, not clearance.

second_rater.rationale: While standard direct-fed microbials are being integrated into commercial feed mill channels and large-scale operations (t002-rumen-consortia_e245, t002-rumen-consortia_e283), engineered rumen consortia face significant organizational hurdles before they can be adopted seamlessly. Key friction points include the lack of feed-mixing facilities and trained personnel on smaller ruminant farms (t002-rumen-consortia_e426), strict storage and transport requirements to keep live biologicals viable (t002-rumen-consortia_e169, t002-rumen-consortia_e286), and a lack of extensive farm-scale validation across diverse management systems (t002-rumen-consortia_e666, t002-rumen-consortia_e670).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The evidence consistently places engineered rumen consortia in a lab-to-field transition phase where integration is described or planned but not yet demonstrated at commercial scale with seamless fit. E670 explicitly states that 'many studies are short-term, small-scale, or conducted in controlled research settings, limiting confidence in their commercial practicality,' and e666 confirms 'broader adoption is constrained by variability across production systems and limited farm-scale validation.' The permanent/semi-permanent colonization model represents a conceptual break from existing daily-additive workflows — rumen fluid collection and inoculation are 'impractical in production settings because collection, preservation, and inoculation are time-consuming and labor-intensive' (e631) — and cold-chain/viability logistics create ongoing organizational friction (e169, e130). Integration pathways are articulated (e679 recommends pairing with 3-NOP; e056 notes strategies must align with existing herd management), and some in situ trials at commercial farms exist (e026, e013), but these require fistulated animals or specialized protocols, indicating moderate-to-major process adaptation is still needed. Knowledge gaps among farm personnel further anchor this at Mid rather than High (e613, e278).

second_rater.rationale: While simple gene-edited microbial products have obtained US registration as soil amendments under USDA APHIS 7 CFR Part 340 (t015-engineered-plant-microbe-consortia_e294, t015-engineered-plant-microbe-consortia_e313), complex engineered plant-microbiome consortia face ongoing navigation challenges due to ecological concerns like horizontal gene transfer (t015-engineered-plant-microbe-consortia_e112, t015-engineered-plant-microbe-consortia_e150). Regulatory pathways exist but require significant effort, with severe restrictions and multi-year timelines under European GMO frameworks compared to more streamlined North American pathways (t015-engineered-plant-microbe-consortia_e266, t015-engineered-plant-microbe-consortia_e320, t015-engineered-plant-microbe-consortia_e333).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Regulatory pathways exist in major jurisdictions but require substantial effort to navigate, placing this technology firmly in the navigation phase. In North America, USDA APHIS 7 CFR Part 340 provides structured permit pathways for engineered microorganisms, and some products (e.g., PROVEN®40, e294) have achieved commercial registration; non-transgenic/gene-edited strains benefit from streamlined notification procedures (e313, e331). EU Regulation 2019/1009 creates a CE marking pathway for microbial fertilising products (e315), and Brazil has codified concentration, purity, and shelf-life standards (e411). However, for GMM-based engineered consortia—the core of this technology—EU Directive 2001/18/EC mandates case-by-case ecological risk assessments and multi-year approval timelines (e320, e333), regulatory uncertainty in Europe is explicitly cited as a competitive threat (e045, e266), and US-specific plant biostimulant/inoculant regulation is still under development via the Plant Biostimulants Act of 2023 (e412, e522). Multiple sources note the absence of dedicated SynCom registration tracks, fragmented global guidelines, and calls for harmonized frameworks (e150, e157, e523, e079), confirming permissions are obtainable with effort but no jurisdiction has granted broad unconditional clearance for engineered (especially transgenic) consortia.

second_rater.rationale: Microbial Electrochemical Systems (MES) currently require specialized expertise in electrochemistry and microbiology (t033-mes_e115), and lack standardized, plug-and-play designs for general staff deployment (t033-mes_e369, t033-mes_e404). However, integration pathways with existing wastewater treatment facilities are well-described (t033-mes_e272, t033-mes_e317), and service-based business models are being used to manage these operational complexities for early industrial adopters (t033-mes_e529).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Evidence consistently describes MES/MET integration as planned or in early demonstration rather than seamless adoption. t033-mes_e432 confirms METs have 'typically been performed on a small scale' with 'only a few devices implemented at larger scale,' and t033-mes_e301 indicates installation timelines of 6–36 months, signaling major organizational effort. t033-mes_e115 identifies requirements for cross-disciplinary expertise (electrochemistry, microbial culturing, potentiostat instrumentation) that current wastewater operators do not possess, while t033-mes_e404 and e407 acknowledge that 'off-the-shelf plug-and-play electrobioreactors' are demanded but not yet widely available. Limited commercial deployments (e.g., Aquacycl BETT at Vopak, t033-mes_e527/e529/e531) show that service-model integration is possible but represent early-stage adaptation, not seamless fit. t033-mes_e272 and e460 describe integration with existing treatment trains as a risk-reduction strategy still under development, confirming the adaptation phase rather than routine embedding.

second_rater.rationale: While bioengineered and selectively bred perennials like Kernza have achieved limited commercial launches through partners like Patagonia and General Mills (t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e104, t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e224, t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e285), they remain niche crops grown on only about 4,000 acres in the U.S. (t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e214). Commercialization is currently characterized by early-adopter participation, supply chain coordination hubs, and ongoing market and yield uncertainties (t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e215, t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e218, t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e287, t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e289, t048-bioengineered-vegetation_e452).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Kernza has clearly moved beyond exploration: commercial products (beer, cereal, flour, pasta, pancake mix) are on shelves at big-box stores nationally, ~50–60 SKUs exist, grower contracts date to 2014, and demand is reported to exceed supply (e224, e421, e434, e117). However, the technology remains explicitly niche and pre-scale: only ~4,000 acres across 36 active growers (e214, e422), yields are 20–40% of annual wheat (e215, e427), farmers cite market/income uncertainty (e452, e453), seed supply is limited and production still described as experimental (e289), and active programs are still working to build supply chains and demonstrate commercial viability (e100, e104, e287, e138). This constellation—limited launches, early-adopter traction, active but incomplete commercialization infrastructure—is characteristic of MRL 5.

second_rater.rationale: Engineered associative nitrogen-fixing microbes, specifically Pivot Bio's PROVEN products (utilizing gene-edited Klebsiella variicola and Kosakonia sacchari), have transitioned from laboratory development to large-scale commercial deployment, covering over 8 million acres of U.S. corn by 2024 (t036-nitrogen-fixing-microbes_e038, t036-nitrogen-fixing-microbes_e176, t036-nitrogen-fixing-microbes_e289, t036-nitrogen-fixing-microbes_e299). Independent field studies and widespread agricultural use demonstrate that this technology is fully functional and integrated into real-world farming practices (t036-nitrogen-fixing-microbes_e328, t036-nitrogen-fixing-microbes_e336).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Pivot Bio's genetically engineered strains (Kv137-1036, with nifL deleted to uncouple nitrogenase expression from ambient nitrogen) have been commercially deployed at massive scale — 3 million acres in 2022 (e289, e299) and 8 million acres in 2024 (e038) — with products sold at $20–24/acre for corn, wheat, barley, and oats (e328, e329). Multiple independent and company-sponsored field trials across multiple seasons and geographies confirm measurable nitrogen delivery (35–40 lb N/acre equivalent) and yield responses (e183, e335, e336, e293), and third-party academic studies have been published (e337). Ginkgo/Bayer R&D (e232–e239) and Kula Bio field trials (e291) represent active next-generation development, while acknowledged limitations — inconsistent field performance, inability to fully replace synthetic nitrogen, and limited peer-reviewed validation of full efficacy claims (e339, e340, e294) — keep the assessment at TRL 8 rather than 9.

second_rater.rationale: mRNA vaccine technology is already commercialized and widely deployed in livestock, specifically swine. Merck Animal Health's Sequivity platform was introduced in 2018 and has been licensed in the US and Canada for customizing swine vaccines, with millions of doses successfully administered to protect against swine pathogens (t060-mrna-vaccines_e102, t060-mrna-vaccines_e147, t060-mrna-vaccines_e161, t060-mrna-vaccines_e394).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The RNA particle/mRNA vaccine technology for livestock is fully commercially deployed. Sequivity (Merck Animal Health) was introduced in 2018, is USDA-licensed for multiple swine applications, and has had over 2 million doses prescribed (e161, e162, e147, e150); field safety was confirmed in ~900 commercial pigs at three U.S. sites and thousands of doses used in Canada since 2014 without safety issues (e089, e090). Additional products built on this platform—SEQUIVITY IAV-S NA (launched 2024), NOBIVAC NXT Canine Flu H3N2, and NOBIVAC NXT FeLV—have reached veterinary clinics (e061, e062, e139, e140), and Merck has committed USD 895 million in manufacturing infrastructure to underpin the line (e196). Cattle-specific mRNA vaccines remain in trials without USDA approval (e071, e188), indicating the platform as applied to beef cattle sits lower, but the core described technology (RNA particle platform exemplified by Sequivity) is operating at full commercial scale.

second_rater.rationale: While the veterinary and agricultural sectors generally support and adopt mRNA livestock vaccines as critical disease-control tools (e.g., t060-mrna-vaccines_e095, t060-mrna-vaccines_e153, t060-mrna-vaccines_e159), there is significant public hesitation and consumer concern. This has led to state-level legislative proposals to ban or label products from animals treated with mRNA vaccines (t060-mrna-vaccines_e151, t060-mrna-vaccines_e277), social media concern about genetics (t060-mrna-vaccines_e311), and some companies prohibiting their use due to consumer backlash (t060-mrna-vaccines_e185).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Evidence presents a bifurcated acceptance landscape. Within the veterinary/livestock professional sector, acceptance is meaningful: veterinarians actively sought access to RNA particle vaccines (e095), Merck's Sequivity is commercially used in thousands of animals without reported safety issues (e089, e090), industry conferences feature the technology (e392), and industry groups (Farm Bureau) support biotechnology policy frameworks (e155, e156). However, substantial societal resistance exists: legislators in at least seven states introduced bills to ban or mandate labeling of mRNA livestock vaccines (e151, e277); consumer concern was sufficient to prompt one company to update protocols prohibiting mRNA vaccines (e185); social media analysis of over 740,000 tweets showed 66.9% perceiving mRNA as unsafe with overall negative sentiment across 44 countries (e308, e310); and a specific discourse cluster (7.1%) explicitly targets mRNA vaccines in the food supply/livestock context with genetic-alteration fears (e311, e303). The opposition is concentrated in identifiable groups (anti-vaccine consumers, conservative legislators) rather than being universal, preventing a Low classification, but it is too organized and widespread to reach High.

second_rater.rationale: Photosynthetic efficiency engineering has moved beyond a theoretical concept into active commercial validation, with companies like ZeaKal partnering with major agricultural players like Dow DuPont to test 'PhotoSeed' technology (e331) and Living Carbon conducting field trials for biomass-enhanced trees (e063). However, widespread commercial sales are not yet realized due to long regulatory approval timelines (e154, e323).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The evidence shows the technology has progressed beyond pure exploration into validation-stage activity: multiple field trials demonstrating yield gains (e033, e451, e501, e063), active commercial development partnerships (ZeaKal with Dow DuPont, e331), Salk's announced commercialization plans (e330), and business-model framing around carbon markets (e091, e092). However, no evidence of actual product launches, sales figures, pricing pages, or customer counts for Calvin cycle / photorespiratory bypass engineered crops is present. On the contrary, e154 explicitly states commercialization of food crops is 'more than a decade' away, and e308 and e323 document substantial regulatory costs ($35M+, 13+ year timelines) and high rates of un-launched engineered crops, firmly blocking expansion-stage readiness.

second_rater.rationale: While growers can use their existing machinery to plant and harvest perennial crops like Kernza (e443), adoption is not yet seamless. Farmers must navigate restrictive trademark licensing processes that initially reject 80% of applicants (e124, e135, e436), manage supply chain bottlenecks and seed delivery delays (e287, e445), and rely on newly established grower cooperatives and peer technical support networks to adapt to the crop's dual-use management requirements (e120, e126).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Evidence confirms that farmers can use existing equipment (e443) and that harvesting skills transfer from grass seed experience (e447), reducing some workflow friction. However, adoption requires significant organizational adaptations: seed supply chains are underdeveloped causing planting delays for all participants (e445), ~80% of applying growers are rejected for lack of alignment, capacity, or equipment (e124), new trademark-licensing agreements must be signed (e436), state-supported technical assistance teams and peer-mentor networks are actively being constructed (e126, e103, e287), and new dual-use grain/forage management paradigms are still being researched (e092, e097). The small scale of adoption (~4,000 U.S. acres, mostly on marginal land as a risk hedge (e214, e441, e442)) and ongoing supply-chain hub formation (e287) confirm the technology is in an active adaptation phase rather than seamless integration.

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The most directly relevant evidence concerns CRISPR editing of cereal crops specifically to enhance recruitment of nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Rice plants were CRISPR-edited to modify the flavone biosynthetic pathway, generating apigenin-enriched roots that stimulated diazotrophic biofilm formation and improved nitrogen fixation and grain yield under low-N conditions (e108, e398, e532). This approach has been extended to wheat, with 2025 results published in Plant Biotechnology Journal showing CRISPR-edited wheat overproducing apigenin, which stimulated nitrogen-fixing bacterial biofilms and improved yields under low-N fertilizer conditions, with a pending patent filed (e199, e206, e207, e210). Similarly, engineered barley was shown to secrete rhizopine to selectively activate nitrogenase in associated diazotrophs (e529). These constitute lab/greenhouse validations of the integrated mechanism (editing → exudate change → bacterial recruitment → measurable yield effect), placing the technology at TRL 3–4. However, no field trial evidence for this specific CRISPR-cereal-recruitment approach is present in the evidence set; e007 and e218 confirm that field demonstration remains outstanding.

entries.tech_name: Genome editing to transfer nitrogen fixation to plants

second_rater.rationale: Transferring the complete nitrogenase pathway (nif operon) directly into plants remains an elusive goal, with major technical challenges such as oxygen sensitivity and high energy requirements still unresolved (t081-n-fixation-plants_e007, t081-n-fixation-plants_e253, t081-n-fixation-plants_e321). While researchers have demonstrated early proof of concept in the lab by expressing functional subcomponents (like the Fe protein via nifH/nifM) in tobacco chloroplasts (t081-n-fixation-plants_e280) and reporting some plastid nitrogenase activity (t081-n-fixation-plants_e317), a fully functional nitrogen-fixing plant has not yet been achieved or tested outside of lab environments (t081-n-fixation-plants_e285, t081-n-fixation-plants_e347).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The evidence consistently confirms that no GM nitrogen-fixing plant has been produced (e007, e253, e285, e347). The most advanced demonstrations involve partial proof-of-concept work: individual nif genes (nifH, nifM) have been expressed in tobacco chloroplasts with in vitro activity only at sub-ambient oxygen (e279, e280, e281, e283), NifDK tetramers have been formed in yeast mitochondria but not replicated in plants (e318, e329, e402), and one company claims nitrogenase activity in plant plastids (e317) but under severely constrained conditions. Critical obstacles remain unresolved—oxygen sensitivity (e010, e186, e282, e336), NifD proteolytic degradation (e344), incomplete cofactor assembly (e345), and the sheer complexity of coordinating 9–20 nif genes in a eukaryotic cell (e130, e286, e337)—confirming the technology has not progressed beyond scientific proof-of-concept for individual components. Evidence about engineered bacteria colonizing plant roots (Pivot Bio, Azotic) represents a distinct approach and was excluded from this assessment.

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Multiple lines of evidence confirm real-world operational deployment of defined nitrifying consortia. Residual gaps include variability in startup times and lag-phase robustness under changing salinity (e421–e423), and the most precisely optimised 'synthetic' assemblies remain under active characterisation (e243–e246, e444–e453), keeping the estimate below TRL 9.

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The evidence overwhelmingly supports High TRL. Multiple commercially deployed products are operating at large scale: Pivot Bio's gene-edited nitrogen-fixing products launched in 2019 and have been applied on tens of millions of acres across North America (e257, e280, e286, e347), with third-party university validation across 14 institutions and 135 on-farm trials demonstrating nitrogen replacement at equivalent yields (e292, e304, e305). Azotic Technologies launched Envita WG in September 2024 (e327), Mammoth P consortium launched in 2015 (e326, e351), and Indigo Ag products are available in the US, Brazil, Argentina, and EU (e432). Replicated multi-year field evidence documents real-world performance (e291, e293, e338, e358). TRL 9 is not reached because persistent challenges remain: season-to-season variability of 14–19.4 kg N/ha for the same commercial product (e318), field-to-field colonization inconsistency across soil types (e355), formulation stability bottlenecks (e356, e357, e365), and independent data showing 51 of 53 corn experiments found no significant yield benefit beyond N-rate alone for some products (e407).

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Multiple lines of evidence confirm that photorespiratory bypass and Calvin-cycle engineering have moved well beyond lab proof-of-concept into replicated field trials across several crops and locations. Specifically, the FD3 bypass produced ~40% biomass gains in tobacco over two growing seasons (e058, e151), up to 35% grain yield gains in rice paddy field trials (e060), and 30% tuber biomass increases in potato field trials (e059, e080, e082); GOC potato trials were conducted across five locations in China over 2019–2024 with 21–69% yield increases (e197, e198). NPQ-acceleration engineering yielded ~33% seed-yield increases in soybean field trials (e033, e451). These results place the technology firmly at TRL 6 (demonstrated in relevant field environment) and touching TRL 7 for the most advanced bypass variants. However, the same literature explicitly cautions that published field studies are 'limited in both number and size,' mostly single-location with small plots and modest replication (e064, e065, e079), multi-environment breeder-style trials are still required (e065), and regulatory approval for food-crop commercial deployment has not been obtained (e029). Commercial deployment therefore has not been achieved, constraining the upper bound to the TRL 6–7 range rather than TRL 8–9.

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Multiple lines of evidence confirm commercial deployment of enzymatic and microbial valorization of agri-food residues. A dataset of 84 companies actively producing upcycled food products has been identified (e382), with named commercial examples such as Upcycled Foods Inc. processing brewers' spent grain into SuperGrain+ flour (e383) and Planetarians converting surplus soy/yeast into plant-based meat alternatives (e384). Commercially available fungal- and bacterial-fermentation-derived food products already exist at scale (e549, e550). Pilot- and industrial-scale evidence is also substantial: a three-stage fermentation system was built and validated at 10 m³ field pilot scale (e103–e104); Aspergillus oryzae α-amylase production from deoiled cakes reached pilot scale in a 600 L fermenter (e152); Rhizopus delemar converted potato-processing waste into SCP at an industrial-scale trial (e135); and industrial acetification in 100 L acetators achieving >94% yield is documented (e140). entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: In the most favorable jurisdictions (USA and Canada), Kernza (intermediate wheatgrass) is already commercially licensed, with USDA Farm Service Agency crop certification, active NRCS conservation payment programs (E328O), and six approved varieties on the market as of 2022 (e065, e221, e222, e284, e424). Jurisdiction variation is substantial: the EU restricts GM cultivation broadly and has no specific clearance for engineered deep-root perennials (e373, e385, e204), India maintains a cautious post-2010 moratorium posture on new GM crops (e349, e372), and New Zealand regulates all GE crops as GMOs (e408). entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The technology is fully operational in the real world. entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The evidence describes integration pathways (seed treatment, soil amendment, fertigation — e398, e416) and some commercial adoption (e392, e242), which takes the technology above a fundamental mismatch. entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The evidence clearly supports a High TRL bin for Engineered Forages. HarvXtra low-lignin alfalfa was commercially released in the USA in 2015 and is described as the 'first and only genetically modified animal forage/feed crop with nutritional enhancement commercialised internationally' (e136), with transgenic low-lignin varieties also noted as broadly commercially available (e85, e86), placing it at TRL 9. HME perennial ryegrass (AgResearch) has completed five years of regulated USDA-APHIS-approved field trials in Missouri, USA, demonstrating translation of elevated leaf fatty acid levels (25–34% above controls) and gross energy gains from lab to field (e139, e144), with in vitro methane reductions of 10–15% confirmed (e145) and endophyte compatibility verified (e150); however, livestock grazing trials in New Zealand have not yet been conducted (e175), placing it at approximately TRL 6–7. The technology as a whole thus spans TRL 7–9 depending on the specific sub-technology.

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: The evidence shows strong laboratory proof-of-concept across multiple bacteria-vector-pathogen combinations (e002, e042, e064, e066, e090–e092, e264), with semi-field cage trials conducted in China (e115, Serratia AS1) and Burkina Faso (e116, e117, e119) and the first semi-field study in large cages for paratransgenic Asaia in anophelines reported (e421–e424). entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Multiple high-quality sources explicitly confirm that no technology-specific regulatory framework for paratransgenic engineered insect symbionts exists anywhere. Evidence e070 states directly that 'laws and regulations need to be created' for genetically modified microorganisms (GMM), and e284 labels regulatory status as 'Unclear.' Real-world field activity is also regressing: related GM mosquito programs have been withdrawn or halted (e391, e405, e407). The combination of absent field-release approvals, an explicitly unclear regulatory status, and the acknowledged need to create new legal instruments places this firmly in the Low bin.

entries.rater_1_rationale_raw: Multiple lines of evidence confirm that CRISPR-mediated S-gene knockout for disease resistance has been validated in multi-year field environments. The StDMR6-1 knockout potato was evaluated in four consecutive field seasons (2020–2023) showing durable broad-spectrum resistance to late blight, early blight, and common scab without yield penalty or tuber quality loss (e169, e170, e172, e368, e323). Wheat S-gene knockouts (TaPsIPK1, TaCIPK14) conferred stripe rust resistance in field trials with no yield penalties (e011), and rice SWEET-gene knockouts producing bacterial blight resistance have been validated across multiple studies (e101, e228, e367, e707). MLO knockouts in wheat (TaMLO, all six alleles) likewise show strong powdery mildew resistance (e010, e102, e227). These represent full system prototypes demonstrated in operational (field) environments across diverse crop species. However, evidence indicates the step from agronomically amenable lab cultivars to commercially important varieties remains underway (e016), and no specifically S-gene KO disease-resistant crop product has yet been commercialized, placing the technology at TRL 7 rather than 8–9.
entries.rater_2_rationale_raw: Multi-year field trials representing real-world operational environments (TRL 7) have been successfully conducted for crops featuring CRISPR-mediated knockouts of susceptibility genes, such as the StDMR6-1 knockout in potatoes evaluated over four years (e169, e323, e368) and TaPsIPK1/TaCIPK14 knockouts in wheat (e011).
